one_liner: Node.js N-API binding to C++ simdjson 0.9; lazyParse beats JSON.parse up to 2.3x by never building JS objects.
what_it_does: An npm native addon (`simdjson`) that wraps simdjson's DOM parser in three functions: isValid(str) returns a boolean, and parse(str) returns a full JS value built through N-API, which its own typings say is slower than JSON.parse. lazyParse(str) returns an object that holds an opaque C++ document plus a valueForKeyPath('a.b[0]') method, which converts only the addressed subtree to JS. The fast path is not a drop-in: property access must be rewritten as key-path strings, and input must be a JS string.
how_it_is_fast: The vendored simdjson 0.9.x parses in two stages: a SIMD pass (AVX2, SSE4.2 or NEON, chosen at runtime) finds structural characters and validates UTF-8, then a second pass writes a compact 64-bit-word 'tape' of the document. lazyParse moves that parsed dom::document into a heap-allocated Napi::External and returns it with no per-value V8 allocation, while JSON.parse builds every object, array and string on the V8 heap. Most of the measured gain is that skipped object construction (issue #5): whenever this binding does build JS objects (parse(), or valueForKeyPath on a large subtree), it adds one property at a time through N-API and loses to JSON.parse.
when_to_use: Large JSON strings (MBs to hundreds of MB) where you read only a few fields with valueForKeyPath. The README shows 2.10x on the 190 MB sf_citylots.json (710 vs 1492 ms).
Number-heavy or geometry documents such as canada.json, marine_ik.json, mesh.json and numbers.json, which the README shows at 1.9-2.3x JSON.parse.

Validation-only gates, where isValid(str) is enough and no JS object is needed. In the maintainer's 2020 run in issue #28 (200k iterations of a 25 KB document), isValid took 5.7 s against JSON.parse's 33.5 s.
An environment you can pin and that builds the addon: Linux x86-64 with a C++17 compiler and an older Node (CI only exercises Node 12.x).
when_not_to_use: You need the whole JS object. parse() and valueForKeyPath('') build it node by node through N-API: 1.7-4x slower than JSON.parse in issue #5's tables, and about 5x slower on a 25 KB document in issue #28.

Many small documents, such as HTTP request bodies of a few KB. Every call copies the JS string to UTF-8, may copy it again into a padded buffer, and allocates a fresh dom::parser, since reusing the parser was never done (open issue #35). Issues #28 and #42 report lazyParse slower than JSON.parse in this pattern.
String-heavy documents: on the README's own table lazyParse loses on twitter.json (0.77x), random.json (0.78x) and citm_catalog.json (0.93x).

Windows, Apple Silicon or current Node. Open issues report MSVC build failures (#44, #52), 'illegal hardware instruction' with an x86_64 Node on an Apple M2 Pro (#70), and node-gyp 6.1.0 failing on Node 20 (#71). There are no prebuilt binaries, and the npm tarball unpacks to 39 MB because the benchmark corpus ships with it (#54).

Production services that need a maintained dependency. Code has not changed since June 2021. A lazyParse memory-leak report (#40, confirmed by a second user in 2022) is still open. Bad key paths can abort the process (see gotchas).

integration.form: module (npm package `simdjson`, an N-API native addon compiled from source by an install script running `node-gyp rebuild`; no prebuilt binaries)
integration.dependencies: node-addon-api ^2.0.0. Building needs node-gyp, Python and a C++17 compiler. simdjson is vendored as the amalgamated simdjson.h/simdjson.cpp (0.9.x; the header declares SIMDJSON_VERSION 0.9.1).
integration.min_toolchain: A C++17 compiler (binding.gyp: -O3 -std=c++17, /std:c++17 on MSVC, C++ exceptions on) and a Node.js with N-API. There is no engines field. CI tests only Node 12.x on ubuntu-latest.
integration.platforms: The vendored simdjson picks a kernel at runtime: x86-64 Haswell (AVX2) or Westmere (SSE4.2), ARM64 (NEON), PPC64, or a portable fallback. The README claims macOS, Linux and Windows, but the Windows (#44, #52) and Apple Silicon (#70) build/run failures are open. The /EHsc workaround for MSVC was suggested in #52 but never merged.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Calls are synchronous, and each one builds its own dom::parser on the stack, so the binding keeps no shared parser state. Use from worker_threads is not documented or tested.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — parse(str) matches JSON.parse(str) without a reviver but is slower than it. The fast lazyParse returns an opaque handle that you read through valueForKeyPath key-path strings, so code has to change.

gotchas: Calling valueForKeyPath with a non-numeric segment where the document has an array (e.g. 'items.name' when items is an array) does not throw a catchable JS error. The binding queues a JS exception, keeps running, and calls std::stoi, whose std::invalid_argument is never caught, so the whole Node process aborts ('terminate called ... what(): stoi', issue #46, reproduced again in 2023).

Key paths are split on '.', '[' and ']' with strtok, and there is no escaping. Keys that contain those characters, such as '@avito-core/toggles:6.1.18' in issue #68, cannot be reached. Every valueForKeyPath call also rebuilds the selected subtree as fresh JS objects, so reading a large subtree costs as much as parse().

If build/Release/simdjson.node is missing (e.g. installed with --ignore-scripts), require('simdjson') silently returns the global JSON object with an isValid function added to it. The global JSON gets modified, and lazyParse is undefined.

It is stricter than JSON.parse and handles input differently. Integers outside the int64/uint64 range fail with a number error (JSON.parse returns an imprecise double), and nesting is capped at 1024 levels. Only JS strings are accepted, so a Buffer must be decoded and is then re-encoded to UTF-8 on every call. Object keys are passed as C strings, so a key containing \u0000 is truncated (a source TODO says 'not 8-bit clean'), and the C++ document's memory is never reported to V8 (no AdjustExternalMemory), so the GC does not see it.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No other Node.js JSON parser is catalogued, and the siblings are libraries for other languages. If you can write your own N-API addon, calling current simdjson (the C++ sibling, v4.x) directly avoids this binding's per-call parser allocation, its DOM-only interface (no On-Demand) and its 2021-era code; orjson and ssrJSON are the Python counterparts and, unlike this binding, return full native objects faster than their stdlib.
verified_claims_summary: The first-party README table (Benchmark.js on a 2018 MacBook Pro, 2.3 GHz Core i9; Node/V8 and compiler versions not stated; addon built at -O3) times simdjson.lazyParse(str), which validates and builds a C++ tape with no JS objects, against JSON.parse(str), which builds the full object graph: 0.77x (twitter.json) to 2.30x (numbers.json), faster on 11 of 15 files, with 2.10x on the 190 MB sf_citylots.json. The results are noisy and fall short of the typings' claim: the same page's ops/sec block shows up to ±192.65% error on JSON.parse, an April 2020 run of the then-master by simdjson maintainer John Keiser (PR #36) had lazyParse slower on 6 of 15 files (mesh.json 0.56x), and the table's 0.20-0.87 GB/s for lazyParse is well below the '> 2.5GB/s' in index.d.ts.
status_note: Abandoned: code last changed on 2021-06-14 (npm 0.9.2, vendoring simdjson 0.9.x while upstream is at v4.6.11), later commits up to 2023-02-23 are dependabot merges only, and the fix PRs sit unmerged (#58 simdjson 2.2.2 was closed, #72 node-gyp is open), but it still gets about 46.8k npm downloads a month and is Apache-2.0 with about 150 lines of binding C++, so a fork onto current simdjson is practical.
